name: PT Murni Sadar Tbk

frontmatter.title: Murni Sadar: paying for the build before it earns
frontmatter.summary: A fast-growing regional hospital group whose expansion is funded with debt while returns on capital stay in low single digits. Growth is real; the cash to pay for it is not yet there. We start at SELL.
thesis: Revenue growth is genuine: the network has reached 11 hospitals and nine-month 2026 sales are running about a fifth above the prior year, on a bed base that is still ramping.
The economics are the problem: return on equity is 3.1% and capex runs at several times depreciation, so the group has posted negative free cash flow in every year since listing.
Leverage carries the build: net debt was IDR747.2bn at the FY2025A balance sheet, about 3.9x EBITDA, it has risen since, and the model needs more borrowing before free cash flow turns.
Our blended value is Rp582 against a market price of Rp855; the price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 35.1% where we model 15.0%.
The shares trade about 13,916,778 rupiah a day against a market value of IDR1,768.6bn, so the liquidity discount is real and a capital raise is the obvious remedy.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: the first clean read on margins after a full year of RS Pejaten
Annual public expose, where management has set out the expansion and technology plan
Dividend decision at the annual meeting; the FY2025 payout was a token amount

blocks.text: We initiate Murni Sadar at **SELL** with a target of **Rp582**, -31.5% from the Rp855 last traded. The company runs 11 private hospitals, has just opened its first Jakarta unit, and is growing revenue at a pace most Indonesian hospital operators have not matched in recent years. That growth is not in dispute. What is in dispute is whether it creates value for shareholders, and on the numbers we can source, it does not yet create enough of it to justify the current price.

The variant view is uncomfortable in both directions. Against the bulls, we do not think the market is wrong about growth; we think it is wrong about the capital intensity that comes with it. Capex has run at roughly a quarter to a third of revenue for four years, free cash flow has been negative throughout, and the gap has been funded with bank debt that has more than doubled since the IPO. Against the bears, we are not arguing the franchise is broken: gross margin is stable around 29.8%, EBITDA margin is 14.1% and rising, and the new units carry higher-acuity cardiac and oncology work that should support pricing over time [S2].

The valuation gap is wide, and it is the heart of the call. Our discounted cash flow, which charges the build programme in full, leaves the equity worth less than nothing before we floor it at zero; the multiple cross-checks value it at Rp1,867 on EV/EBITDA and Rp475 on earnings. Two figures are often run together in this kind of report and we keep them apart. The method blend — each method at its weight, before the scenario probabilities are applied — is Rp608 a share, or Rp680 once the house roll-forward to the target date is added. The probability-weighted scenario value is Rp831, which sits above the blend because the bull branch is the only one the method set lets move; the liquidity discount of 30.0% that the house applies to a stock this thin then brings the target to Rp582 [S0]. We weight the cash flow method most heavily because it is the only one that sees the capex, so the target is in practice carried by the multiples; we say that plainly rather than let the weighting imply a precision the cash flow cannot support.

Three things carry the value in the bull branch, the only branch in which the cash flow is not floored. The first is the capex ratio: if the build normalises faster than we assume, the equity is worth materially more. The second is the margin on the enlarged bed base, because a hospital that opens at a loss and matures at a group margin is a different asset from one that never matures. The third is financing: on the FY2025A accounts net debt was 3.9x EBITDA with interest cover a little over two times on the same basis, that leverage has risen again at the September 2026 balance sheet, and the group has limited room to absorb a slip in the ramp before it needs new equity [S0]. We would rather own this after the capital structure is fixed than before.

Murni Sadar is an Indonesian private hospital operator. The group describes itself as providing health services and managing private hospitals, with outpatient clinics, laboratory and blood-bank work, radiotherapy, radiology, a heart and vascular centre, endoscopy and medical rehabilitation among its service lines [S0]. In practice it is a secondary and tertiary hospital network built around a flagship in North Sumatra that has been extended into Java and into higher-acuity work.

The network reached 11 hospitals at the end of FY2025, up from ten a year earlier, as management reported at the June 2026 public expose [S2]. The newest unit is RS Murni Teguh Pejaten in South Jakarta, which opened in September 2025 with 100 beds and room to double that count, and which is positioned on cardiovascular and oncology work rather than general medicine [S12]. That is the strategic bet in one building: move from a regional general hospital group, where tariffs are set largely by the national insurer and competition is local, to a Jakarta specialist centre where private pay and complex cases support a better revenue per bed.

The larger project is at home. Construction of RS Murni Teguh Gama City in Deli Serdang began with piling in February 2025: a 15-storey building on more than 2 hectares at CitraLand Gama City, designed for 1,000 beds and built in stages, with a cyclotron that management describes as the first outside Java [S13]. Management presented it as relief for the full Medan flagship rather than as a Jakarta-style specialist bet [S13]. For the model this is the single most important capital fact: a project of that size is a multi-year capex programme, and it is why the capex ratio stays at the demonstrated level through FY2027E instead of falling once Pejaten is equipped.

Management's stated priorities are stem-cell therapy, robotic surgery, artificial intelligence in diagnostics and administration, and continued network expansion [S2]. The company has installed robotic surgery and a LINAC and PET scan at the Jakarta unit, and it frames the investment as import substitution for Indonesians who currently travel abroad for complex treatment [S12]. This is a plausible strategy and it is also an expensive one: robotic platforms, linear accelerators and PET scanners are capital items with long payback periods, which is why the capex line has not fallen as revenue has grown.

The revenue base is broad rather than concentrated. Inpatient and outpatient care, pharmacy, laboratory and diagnostics all contribute, and no single payer disclosure in the public material suggests dependence on one corporate client [S2]. The group employed 4,157.0 people at the last count [S0]. Scale is mid-tier: it is larger than a single-site operator but far smaller than the listed national chains, which puts it in the challenger group that has to compete for consultants, nurses and payer contracts without the procurement leverage of the leaders.

Ownership is the defining structural fact. The data pack puts the free float at 11.8% and insider holdings at 95.0%; the two cannot both be right because together they exceed the whole share count, so we use the float, which is consistent with the traded value and the market capitalisation, and read the rest of the register as family and affiliate control rather than as a measured insider total [S0]. The founding family's control is stable and has not been diluted since listing, and there has been no rights issue or buyback; the share count has been constant [S0]. For a minority holder this cuts both ways: control is aligned with a long-term build, but there is no external check on capital allocation and very little stock available to trade — the three-month average daily traded value is 13,916,778 rupiah [S0].

Murni Teguh began as a single hospital in Medan and grew by adding units in North Sumatra before moving into Java. Indonesian private hospitals typically earn most of their revenue from inpatient stays and procedures, with doctors working as independent contractors rather than employees, which keeps fixed costs lower than in many other markets but gives consultants bargaining power over where they admit patients. The national health insurer is the largest single payer in the system, and its tariff schedule sets a reference price that private operators must beat with service quality or private-pay mix. The regulatory direction of travel has been toward standardised service classes and tighter tariff rules, which compresses the room for premium pricing in general wards and rewards operators that can shift their case mix toward specialist work.

Indonesian hospital demand is driven by three things that are not going away: a large and ageing population, under-provision of beds relative to the region, and the steady formalisation of health financing through the national insurer. For a listed operator the practical question is not whether demand grows but who captures it and at what price. The macro deck we use has Indonesian real GDP growing 5.3% in FY2027E with inflation of 3.3%, which is the nominal spending backdrop the sector plans against [S0].

Policy is the swing factor. The health omnibus law and its implementing regulations pushed the system toward standardised inpatient classes, replacing the old three-class structure with a single tier defined by service standards. For operators this removes some of the ability to segment wards by price and pushes competition toward case mix, clinical outcomes and payer contracts. It also raises the minimum service specification for every bed, which means renovation capex for older buildings. We treat this as a structural cost rather than a one-off, and it is one reason we do not assume margins expand quickly in the general-ward business.

Competitive position is best described as regional strength, national challenger. In North Sumatra the group is a reference provider with a long-standing consultant base; in Jakarta it is a new entrant with a single specialist unit competing against established national chains and against the city's own teaching hospitals. The Jakarta unit's differentiation is equipment and the cardiac and oncology focus rather than price, and it will need a few years of consultant recruitment before it fills [S12]. Market share in a fragmented national market is small in absolute terms, and the group does not publish a share figure in the material we could source.

The moat, such as it is, is local. Hospital competition is a travel-distance business: patients choose the nearest credible provider for everything except complex procedures, so a well-run regional hospital has a genuine catchment advantage that a new entrant cannot buy quickly. Switching costs are moderate for chronic care and low for one-off diagnostics. Against that, the group's ability to raise prices is constrained by the insurer, and its ability to win consultants depends on equipment and operating theatres, which is exactly where the capex goes [S12].

Five forces leave the industry attractive on demand but crowded on returns. Supplier power is high for equipment and for scarce specialists; buyer power is high because the national insurer sets tariffs for a large share of admissions; the threat of new entrants is real in Jakarta and low in secondary towns; substitutes are limited but medical tourism removes high-value cases; and rivalry is intensifying as listed chains and private equity-backed groups add beds. The result is an industry that grows revenue reliably and earns mediocre returns on capital unless the operator has either scale or a defensible specialist franchise. Murni Sadar has neither yet at national scale.

External influences are mostly second-order. The rupiah matters for imported equipment and drugs rather than for revenue, and the macro deck has the currency at 18,350 to the dollar in FY2027E, so equipment costs stay high in local terms [S0]. Rates matter more: the policy rate is put at 5.8% in the same deck, and a leveraged hospital group with a variable-rate loan book is directly exposed to it [S0]. Regulation is the largest single external risk, and we return to it in section five. We could not archive the implementing regulation itself, so the policy discussion in the background block above is general knowledge; it shapes how we read the industry but it is not used to set any scenario weight.

The historical record shows a company that grew steadily and earned almost nothing until very recently. Revenue went from IDR822.3bn in FY2022A to IDR1,357.9bn in FY2025A, a compound rate in the high teens, while net profit swung from IDR66.0bn to a small loss in FY2023A and only IDR43.6bn in FY2025A [S0]. The FY2025 recovery is the important data point: EBITDA rose to IDR191.6bn at a 14.1% margin, roughly double the prior year, as revenue growth outran fixed costs.

The FY2026 run rate is the strongest evidence the operating leverage story is working. Nine-month revenue is about a fifth above the same period of 2025, with each quarter setting a new high, and the third quarter alone produced an EBITDA margin above the full-year FY2025 figure [S0]. Our FY2026E build takes revenue to IDR1,643.0bn, an increase of 21.0%, and holds the gross margin at 31.6% with SG&A at 19.5% of sales, close to what the accounts show for FY2025A and the first nine months of 2026 [S0]. That produces EBITDA of IDR297.4bn and a net margin of 4.7%. Management's own target for the year is growth of a fifth, which our build matches [S9].

The anchor for that build is interim, and that matters more than the growth rate. FY2026E is struck on the nine months to September 2026 — the most recent figures in the pack, but unaudited and unreviewed — and it assumes the December quarter trades at the nine-month economics rather than repeating a year-end true-up. The assumption is doing real work: IDR297.4bn of EBITDA for the year, against the nine months already reported, requires a December-quarter EBITDA margin of about nineteen per cent, whereas the only December quarter in the audited record earned three and a half per cent and a net loss [S0]. We could not source any explanation of what drove that FY2025 charge, so we neither declare it non-recurring nor mechanise it: the base case carries the nine-month run rate, and the bear case is floored and cannot express the difference. The earnings-quality screen weights interim anchors against the audited full year for exactly this reason, which is why we call the FY2026E margin the least evidenced line in the model. If the true-up recurs, FY2026E EBITDA is overstated and the bull branch — the only branch with a positive cash flow — is where the published value would fall; we say that rather than let a floored scenario set imply the risk is captured.

Costs are dominated by medical consumables, doctor fees and staff. Gross margin has been broadly stable since the start of FY2025, which tells us the group is not buying growth with discounts; the pressure instead comes below the gross line, where new hospitals carry opening costs and where depreciation rises with every completed building. Our model lifts the gross margin modestly to 32.0% by FY2030E on the higher-acuity mix management is targeting, and trims SG&A to 19.5% on the procurement and energy programmes cited at the public expose [S2]. We do not assume a step change in profitability, because the last three years do not support one.

Cash flow is where the story turns uncomfortable. Operating cash flow has been positive and growing, but capex has been larger every year, so free cash flow has been negative since listing [S0]. In FY2025A the group spent IDR352.2bn on capex against depreciation of IDR77.4bn, a ratio of roughly four and a half times, and the twelve months to September 2026 show the same pattern with capex above operating cash flow again [S0]. We model the ratio falling from 30.0% of revenue in FY2026E to 15.0% by FY2030E and to 11.0% by FY2035E. The ratio is a group-wide charge and includes the Gama City build [S13]; it holds the demonstrated level through FY2027E, and the later step-down is a balance-sheet constraint, not a dated project calendar, because capex at 25.9% of revenue and above EBITDA cannot be debt-funded indefinitely [S0]. Even on that path the terminal ratio stays above the depreciation charge rather than below it: it funds replacement plus the growth capital the terminal growth rate requires. Free cash flow to the firm only turns positive in FY2031E, at IDR72.2bn, and stays thin.

Working capital is a small positive rather than a drag. The group runs negative operating working capital of about -2.9% of revenue, because patient prepayments and supplier terms exceed receivables, so growth releases a little cash rather than absorbing it [S0]. Receivables have grown more slowly than revenue, which is the right direction, and inventory is a minor line for a service business. The working-capital line is not where the cash goes.

The balance sheet is where it does. Net debt reached IDR747.2bn at the end of FY2025A, or 3.9x EBITDA, and the September 2026 balance sheet shows debt still climbing as the build continues [S0]. On the same FY2025A accounts, EBIT of IDR114.2bn covered interest of IDR53.2bn a little over two times; the twelve months to September 2026 carry a larger debt stock and a heavier interest bill, so the relationship should not be read as having improved with the growth. The facility terms, covenants and maturity profile are not disclosed in the material we could source, which is a gap a creditor should test rather than a reassurance [S0]. Our forecast has net debt peaking at IDR2,222.8bn in FY2033E, not when free cash flow to the firm first turns positive in FY2031E: from then on the after-tax interest bill and the dividend absorb more than the free cash flow before capex falls further. That is a capital structure that leaves no room for a bad year.

Capital allocation has been single-minded: every rupiah of internal cash and a growing pile of borrowings has gone into buildings and equipment. The dividend is token: the FY2025 dividend was Rp2.42 a share, an 11.5% payout on FY2025 EPS, and it was paid in June 2026 out of FY2025 earnings [S0]. We carry a similar 10.0% payout forward, which is a forward DPS of Rp3.76 and is not the dividend that was paid. We do not read the payout as a signal of confidence; we read it as the minimum needed to keep the stock investable for domestic funds.

Earnings quality screens come out clean on the accrual measure and mixed on the structural ones. Net profit has been below operating cash flow in each of the last two years, which is the opposite of the accrual warning sign, and there is no evidence of receivables or inventory outrunning sales [S0]. The concerns are structural rather than accounting: capitalised interest and development costs are not disclosed in the material we could source, depreciation is small relative to the asset base because so much of the spend is recent, and the effective tax rate of 40.4% is well above the statutory rate, which points to non-deductible costs that will persist [S0]. We flag the depreciation point explicitly: the data we use shows a charge of about six per cent of revenue, and a hospital group with a newer asset base would normally carry more. If the true charge is higher, EBITDA is overstated and the multiple cross-check is flattered; the cash flow method is unaffected because it charges the capex directly.

Hospital accounting has two features that matter for outside analysis. First, depreciation on buildings and medical equipment is a real cost but a slow one, so a group in a build phase looks profitable on EBITDA long before it looks profitable on earnings. Second, the direct cash-flow method used in Indonesian filings does not always present depreciation as a separate line, so data vendors reconstruct it and frequently understate it. The practical remedy is to read the fixed-asset note, which we could not obtain for this company, and to treat any EBITDA figure built from a reconstructed depreciation charge as an upper bound.

We value Murni Sadar on free cash flow to the firm as the primary method, with EV/EBITDA and price-to-earnings as cross-checks, weighted 60.0% / 30.0% / 10.0% following the house hospital template [S0]. The weighting is deliberate. For a company where capex is several times depreciation and rising, earnings-based methods flatter the value, because accounting profit does not see the cash that goes into the ground. The cash flow method is the only one that does.

The discount rate is built bottom-up. A risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5% and a 1.6% sovereign default spread subtracted from the sum give a cost of equity of 12.6% on an unlevered beta of 0.70, re-levered to 1.02: 7.4% + 1.02 × 4.2% + 2.5% − 1.6% = 12.6%. With pre-tax debt at 9.4%, a 22.0% marginal rate and weights of 63.4% equity and 36.6% debt at a 0.58 debt-to-equity ratio, the weighted average cost of capital is 10.7% [S0].

We have to argue 10.7% against the house compounder card's eleven-to-thirteen per cent band for rupiah cash flows, because it sits below it. The band is a cost-of-capital anchor and the cost of equity of 12.6% is inside it; the blended rate lands lower only because the group's debt is carried at a 9.4% pre-tax book rate that is cheap relative to the equity it substitutes for, and because the 22.0% tax shield is taken at the statutory rather than the much higher effective rate the group actually pays. We keep the engine's bottom-up build rather than force the number into the band. The direction of that choice runs against the rating, not for it, and an earlier version of this paragraph had it backwards. Because the base-case cash-flow leg is floored at zero, the base target is invariant to the discount rate: the cost-of-capital and terminal-growth grid in the sensitivity table is zero in every cell, so moving the rate up or down changes a number that is already zero. The only branch the rate moves is the bull case, and it is valued at nine point seven per cent — a full point below the base rate and therefore more than a point below the band floor — so a rate at the floor would lower the bull value, and with it the probability-weighted Rp831 and the Rp582 target. The sub-band rate therefore flatters the target rather than penalising it, and the honest reading is that the SELL would be deeper, not shallower, at the band floor. We do not restate the model to force that: the base value is carried by the frozen multiples, the change would land entirely in a scenario whose probability is a judgment, and the direction is disclosed instead. The scenario set moves the cost of capital in both directions by the same amount, so the band argument does not change the ranking of the scenarios.

The discounted cash flow produces an enterprise value of IDR19.5bn, which after net debt and minorities leaves negative equity; we floor the share value at zero rather than publish a negative price, because a shareholder's liability is limited [S0]. The shape of that number is the story: the explicit forecast period is cash-negative because the group is still building, so the enterprise value the model produces is smaller than the terminal value it contains. The engine's terminal-value ratio of 23.1x is discounted terminal value divided by that thin enterprise value, not a percentage of value that is terminal; it is a warning that the whole enterprise value rests on the terminal assumptions, not a healthy value split. Those assumptions are a growth rate of 2.5%, a terminal capex ratio of 11.0% of revenue that stays above the 6.0% depreciation charge, and a terminal return on invested capital below the cost of capital of 10.7%. The mechanism is the step-down in capex from the build peak, not capex falling below depreciation: free cash flow turns because the capex ratio more than halves, while the remaining capex still exceeds D&A. Terminal returns stay below the cost of capital, so the growth carried in the perpetuity is not free and we claim no moat that would justify it; how much that growth is worth, and which way the convention cuts, is set out two paragraphs below. The cash flow method is a floor test, not a price: it says that the build, funded as it is, does not return its cost of capital within the horizon we can see.

The multiple-survival test is the discipline the compounder card makes mandatory, and on these numbers the DCF asks a future owner to pay a fraction of what we pay today. The perpetuity that carries the enterprise value, divided by the FY2035E EBITDA of IDR645.4bn it capitalises, implies an exit of about one point eight turns of that year's EBITDA and about two point six turns of its EBIT of IDR436.1bn. At Rp855 the same assets trade at roughly twelve point four times last-twelve-month EBITDA, so the exit is about a seventh of the entry multiple [S0]. That is multiple compression inside the DCF rather than multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume, and it is a statement about the asset rather than about sentiment: if the build is worth less than it costs, the terminal business is worth less per unit of EBITDA than the business the market buys today.

Growth here is manufactured, not declared, and the card's identity is growth = reinvestment × return on incremental capital. In the terminal year net reinvestment is IDR383.8bn of capex less IDR209.3bn of depreciation, about five per cent of the IDR3,488.7bn of revenue that year and about two-thirds of after-tax operating profit at the 40.4% effective rate. On those inputs the terminal year funds the 2.5% growth rate only at an incremental return of roughly three point seven per cent, about a third of the 10.7% cost of capital. Put the other way: to hold that growth the group keeps two-thirds of its profit inside the business and earns under four per cent on it, which is the arithmetic of a franchise that has not reached its cost of capital, not of one with a moat that will take it there [S0].

The terminal growth needs a correction of emphasis, because an earlier draft of this report said the growth rate added nothing. Inside the engine's Gordon convention the perpetuity is struck on FY2035E free cash flow of IDR91.2bn: capitalised at the 10.7% cost of capital with no growth, the terminal value would be about a quarter lower, so the 2.5% rate lifts the zero-growth figure by about a third, and we should say that rather than the reverse [S0]. The economics still run the other way. On the card's value-driver identity, which charges the growth its reinvestment, the same inputs give a terminal value roughly a tenth below the Gordon figure, and a terminal year with no growth at all — replacement capex only, profit no longer split with a sub-cost project — would be worth more than either. What stops that arithmetic from moving the call is the floor: the explicit period consumes more than any of those terminal readings add back, the equity value is negative in all three, and the published value of Rp0 is unchanged. We keep the engine's convention, disclose that it is the generous one, and note that the whole dispute is below zero.

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is the finding. At 21.6x EV/EBITDA the multiple method gives Rp1,867 a share, and at 19.8x earnings the P/E method gives Rp475, against a cash flow value below zero before the floor. Both capitalise a last-twelve-month profit measure struck before the capex the company actually spends, and both use a benchmark that blends the peer median with our own four-year trading history, a mean inflated by a year when EBITDA was a fraction of today's level [S0]. We keep the weights because the multiples are the only methods with a positive, observable base and because they are what this market pays for hospital growth, but we treat them as a ceiling on value rather than as a value: the 30.0% weight on the EV/EBITDA cross-check is a cross-check weight, not an endorsement of a 21.6x multiple. The divergence is disclosed in the valuation table and is the single largest judgment in this report.

Applying those weights on the base case gives Rp608 a share before the liquidity discount, of which the cash flow method contributes nothing and the EV/EBITDA cross-check close to all of it. Weighting the three scenarios at their probabilities raises the figure to Rp831, and the house liquidity discount of 30.0% brings the target to Rp582 [S0]. The discount is not a comment on the business; it is a comment on the fact that the free float is 11.8% and the three-month average daily traded value is 13,916,778 rupiah, so a large buyer cannot build or exit a position without moving the price [S0].

The market has already marked the build down. At Rp855 the shares sit close to the low of their last-year range, Rp800, and far below its high of Rp1,390 [S0], and the multiple the market pays on trailing EBITDA is a fraction of what this company was awarded in its first years as a listed builder. That matters for the buy case: a de-rating of this size already prices in some of the capex doubt. It does not soften the rating, which is SELL: the target of Rp582 sits -31.5% from the price, and that gap, not the scenario weights, is what carries the call. It does mean the stock does not need perfection to stop falling, only evidence that the capex is ending.

The scenario ordering is inverted, and the table should be read with that in front of it rather than as a mild downside case. The bear value of Rp681 is a rupiah ABOVE the base of Rp680, which the engine flags and we do not disguise. The cause is mechanical: the two multiple legs are struck on last-twelve-month EBITDA and parent profit that no forecast shock touches, and the cash-flow equity is negative and floored at zero in both the base and the bear case, so the only difference between the two is the dividend deduction in the total-payout formula. Two things follow, and neither is comfortable for the target. The probability-weighted value cannot be read as a risk-adjusted value, because one of its three branches carries no downside expression at all; and the bear case understates rather than measures the downside, since a slower ramp, a thinner margin and a higher cost of capital all land on a cash-flow value that is already zero. What sets the bear case here is the floor, not the franchise [S0].

The bull case is built from the beds rather than from a margin uplift. RS Pejaten opened with 100 beds and the group's own plan is to develop the site to 200 [S12]; we treat the additional capacity as fit-out and equipment inside the existing development rather than as a second greenfield site, which is why the bull case needs equipment capex but not new land. Our bull case has that capacity fill on the group's revenue per bed over the forecast period, with the cardiac and oncology mix holding the higher gross margin and capex falling away once it is equipped. We cannot source a revenue-per-bed figure from the public material, so we do not publish one; that is a genuine limit on the precision of the bull case and the reason we keep its probability at one quarter.

What does the current price imply? Running the model backwards, Rp855 requires FY2027E revenue growth of 35.1%, against the 15.0% we forecast, holding everything else at our base case [S0]. That is not a wild number for a company that has just grown in the high teens, and it is why we are not aggressively negative: the market is pricing a good year, not a fantasy. But it is pricing that good year with no discount for the capex or the leverage, and that is where we part company.

The sensitivity table should be read as a test of this model's arithmetic, not as a map of the economics, because the floor governs both grids. The first grid — DCF value per share against the cost of capital and terminal growth — is zero in every one of its cells: the cash-flow equity is floored at zero before either input can bite, so a different discount rate or growth rate moves a number that is already zero. The second — twelve-month value on the base case against revenue growth and gross margin — spans a rupiah or two around the Rp680 base target, and its slope runs the wrong way for a useful sensitivity. In every cell a better operating outcome makes the base-case target a fraction lower, because the two multiple legs are frozen on last-twelve-month EBITDA and parent profit that no forecast shock touches, the cash-flow leg is floored, and the only thing that moves is the forward dividend that the total-return formula deducts: a larger dividend is netted off against a value that does not otherwise change. A two-point difference in growth is therefore worth about a tenth of a rupiah, not a fifth of the value; an earlier draft's claim that growth, margin and capex move the value by double-digit percentages described a run on the unfloored cash flow, which is not the model delivered here. What a floored DCF means for sensitivity is that the base case cannot show how value responds to the operating drivers except through that dividend effect — the floor, not the forecast, sets the answer. Those drivers do reach the published target, but only through the bull branch, the sole case in which the cash flow is positive and unfloored, which is why the target moves with the bull probability rather than with any single operating shock. Capex, the variable we would actually watch, appears in neither grid: it is felt through the year the cash flow turns positive and through the bull case, and it cannot be read off these tables. That is a weakness of a floored model, and it is why section five leans on the scenario spread rather than on this table.

The first risk is financing. On the FY2025A accounts net debt is 3.9x EBITDA and EBIT covers interest a little over two times; the September 2026 balance sheet shows net debt higher again, so leverage has not fallen with the growth, and the forecast needs more borrowing before free cash flow turns [S0]. A rise in the policy rate, which the macro deck puts at 5.8% in FY2027E, flows straight through a variable-rate loan book [S0]. Likelihood: medium. Impact: high. This is the risk that would force a rights issue at a price minority holders would not choose.

We do not run a separate refinancing case, and that is a choice rather than an omission. The cash-flow consequence of a tighter facility is already in the bear case through a higher cost of capital and a capex ratio that stays at the demonstrated level. What is not modelled is a rights issue, because no facility is disclosed as maturing, no covenant breach is disclosed, and we could not date or price an equity raise from the material we could source [S0]. We flag that as a gap instead of inventing a trigger. If the facility were not renewed, the dilution would land at a discount to a market price that already sits below our unweighted blend, which is the outcome a minority holder should fear most.

The second is execution on the new units. RS Pejaten opened with 100 beds and is positioned on cardiac and oncology work that requires consultant recruitment and payer contracts before it fills [S12]. Hospitals typically take several years to reach group margins, and a slower ramp would hit both revenue and the fixed-cost absorption that the FY2025 margin recovery depends on. Likelihood: medium. Impact: medium to high.

The third is regulation and tariff. The move to standardised inpatient classes compresses the price differentiation that private operators used to rely on, and the national insurer remains the reference payer for a large share of admissions. A tightening of tariff rules or a change in the class standard would hit revenue per bed across the network at once. We could not source the implementing regulation, so this risk is argued from general knowledge and is deliberately not one of the shocks in the scenarios. Likelihood: medium. Impact: medium.

The fourth is liquidity. The free float is 11.8% and the three-month average daily traded value is 13,916,778 rupiah [S0]. Passive demand is negligible at this size, the traded value is thin, and the exit is narrow. That is a permanent feature of the investment case rather than a temporary technical, and it is why the house applies a 30.0% discount rather than a haircut to the estimates. Likelihood: certain. Impact: medium, mostly on the discount rate rather than on the business.

The fifth is governance and related parties. Control sits with the founding family, the board is family-influenced, and we could not obtain the filings that would let us quantify related-party flows or identify affiliates, so we treat the disclosure as thin rather than clean [S0]. Likelihood of a value-destroying transaction: low to medium in any single year, higher over a decade of build. Impact: medium.

Our base case, at 50.0% probability, is the path described above: high-teens growth fading to ten per cent by FY2030E, a modest margin improvement, and capex normalising after the current projects. It values the equity at Rp680. The bear case, at 25.0%, slows the ramp, compresses the gross margin, carries a December true-up of the FY2025 kind and keeps capex high for longer, and values the equity at Rp681. The bull case, at 25.0%, fills the new beds faster, lifts the margin on the higher-acuity mix and lets capex fall away sooner, and values the equity at Rp1,281. The shocks are mirrored in size, but their reach is not: the cash flow is the only method the scenarios move, because the two multiples are struck on last-twelve-month EBITDA and profit that no forecast shock can change, and on the base and bear cases the cash flow equity is negative and floored at zero. The bear case therefore cannot fall below the base case at all: it sits a rupiah above it, and the bull case is the only one in which the cash flow turns positive. That is why the probability-weighted value sits above the base case, and it is a property of the method set rather than a claim about risk. It also tells you where the target's sensitivity really sits: with base and bear within a rupiah of each other, the pre-discount blend of Rp831 is the base value of Rp680 plus the 25.0% bull weight applied to the gap between Rp1,281 and the base, so the bull probability moves the target more than any single operating shock. We treat the spread as evidence of how little of the value we can see, not as a balanced risk-reward.

Signposts that would change our view: a fall in the capex-to-revenue ratio below our path without a corresponding slowdown in revenue; a gross margin sustained above thirty-two per cent for two quarters; a capital raise that fixes the balance sheet and the free float at the same time; or a disposal or partnership that brings in cash without giving up the flagship. On the other side, a further rise in net debt to EBITDA from here, a dividend cut, or a delay to the Jakarta ramp would push us toward the bear case.

Ownership is concentrated and stable. The data pack reports a free float of 11.8% and insider holdings of 95.0%, figures that sum past the whole share count and therefore cannot both be correct; we use the float, which is consistent with the traded value, and describe the rest of the register as family and affiliate control rather than rely on the insider total [S0]. The listing has not been used to raise fresh equity: the share count has been constant at 2,068.5 million shares since the IPO, and there has been no rights issue or buyback [S0]. Control is therefore exercised with the family's own capital, which aligns incentives with the long build but leaves minority holders with no voice.

The float has a direct market consequence. With 11.8% of the shares available and 13,916,778 rupiah traded on an average day, the stock is too thin for most institutional mandates at a market capitalisation of IDR1,768.6bn [S0]. For governance purposes the important point is not the index mechanics but the incentive it creates: the cheapest way to widen the register is to sell shares or issue new ones, and a capital raise is the most likely remedy over the next few years.

Related-party disclosure is the weakest part of the file we could assemble. We could not obtain the annual report notes that would let us put a number on related-party revenue, purchases or balances, so we classify this as unquantified rather than resolved. Pledged shares, auditor identity, any audit qualification and the IDX board or notation status are likewise not in the material we could source, so we assert nothing about any of them. The balance sheet shows no indication of distress, and nothing in the pack we hold contradicts that read [S0]. We flag these gaps rather than assume them away.

The dividend record is short and small. The group paid Rp2.42 a share in June 2026 out of FY2025 earnings, an 11.5% payout, and did not pay dividends in the two prior years [S0]. The model's forward DPS is Rp3.76 at a 10.0% payout, which is a forecast and not the dividend that was paid. With capex above operating cash flow, a large distribution would be imprudent, and we do not expect one. ESG exposures are typical for the sector: medical and hazardous waste handling, energy use in large buildings, clinical waste from oncology treatment, and labour practices for nurses and support staff. The public material emphasises energy savings and technology adoption rather than environmental targets [S2]. On the social side, the group's dependence on the national insurer gives it a role in access to care that regulators watch closely, and its staffing model depends on a constrained supply of specialists.

The calendar is sparse and that is itself a feature of a small-cap with a thin float. The FY2026 audited accounts, due within four months of the year end, will be the first full-year read on the Jakarta unit and on whether the FY2025 margin recovery held through a year of expansion [S2]. The annual public expose in June is where management has historically set out the expansion and technology plan, and where the 2026 edition flagged stem-cell, robotic surgery and network growth as the priorities [S2]. The dividend decision at the same meeting will show whether the board prioritises deleveraging or distribution [S0].

Between those dates we watch four numbers. Revenue growth against the high-teens run rate tells us whether the new beds are filling. Gross margin tells us whether the higher-acuity mix is translating into pricing. Capex as a share of revenue tells us whether the build is ending. And net debt to EBITDA tells us how much room the balance sheet has left [S0]. We would also track the free float and any announcement of a capital raise, because the low float is structural and a solution would change both the discount rate and the share count [S0].

valuation.label: EV/EBITDA
valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

bear.narrative: New hospitals ramp slowly, opening costs and consumable inflation hold gross margin below the 2026 level, the December quarter repeats the FY2025 year-end true-up so the full year undershoots the nine-month run rate, capex stays at the demonstrated 30% of revenue, and refinancing at a higher rate lifts the cost of capital, so free cash flow stays negative and debt keeps rising.

bull.narrative: Pejaten fills toward its expanded bed count faster than planned, the cardiac and oncology mix lifts gross margin, capex falls away sooner and refinancing comes a point cheaper, so the group starts deleveraging from a larger EBITDA base.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E reproduces the 9M-2026 run rate: nine-month revenue is up about a fifth year on year on a higher bed base, with RS Pejaten (11th unit, opened Sep 2025) ramping; FY2027E-FY2030E fade as the new Jakarta unit ramps and management targets 20% growth for 2026 rather than adding whole new cities every year [S2, S9].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the 9M-2026 actual gross margin of 31.6% (Rp384.6bn on Rp1,215.6bn) rather than FY2025A 29.9%, because the reported nine months is the most recent demonstrated economics; the small further gain reflects the higher-acuity cardiac and oncology mix at Pejaten, not a cost cut [S0, S12].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the 9M-2026 reported SG&A ratio of 19.5% of revenue, which is the last demonstrated level and already reflects the energy-efficiency programme management cited at the public expose; held flat rather than reverting to the FY2025A 21.4% [S0, S2].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: LTM D&A is 5.8% of revenue and rises with the new buildings and equipment; held at 6.0% of revenue, in line with the reported charge rather than the opening PPE stock [S0].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: The modelled path is 30% / 28% / 24% / 19% / 15% of revenue in FY2026E-FY2030E and 11% from FY2031E. FY2026E holds the 9M-2026 actual 30% and FY2027E holds 28% because the Gama City project (1,000 beds, 15 floors, staged build started February 2025) is in construction alongside the Pejaten ramp [S13, S0]; FY2025A was 25.9%. The step-down from FY2028E is not a project calendar but the balance-sheet constraint: capex has exceeded EBITDA and net debt is around 4x, so a ratio at the FY2025A level cannot be debt-funded indefinitely [S0]. The 11% terminal ratio is built as 6.0% D&A plus about 4pp of growth capital (terminal growth 2.5% x the FY2024A-FY2025A average incremental capex/revenue of about 1.6x) plus 1pp for the higher-acuity equipment refresh (cyclotron, PET, robotic surgery); at 11% it remains 1.83x D&A, i.e. above replacement, so no year assumes capex below depreciation [S0, S13].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Engine default from the FY2023A-FY2025A average: hospital working capital runs slightly negative because patient prepayments and supplier terms exceed receivables [S0].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The LK effective rate: FY2025A tax of Rp29.18bn on pre-tax Rp72.27bn is 40.4%, and FY2024 was 72.4% on a small base; the three-year aggregate is 55.0%, so the earlier 30% claim was wrong. We hold the last actual 40.4% because the non-deductible costs persist, against the 22% statutory rate used in the WACC [S0].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Engine default from FY2023A-FY2025A: reported interest expense over opening gross debt, which is what the pack's income statement and balance sheet support. The facility terms, bank counterparties and maturities are not disclosed in the material we could source, so no named lender is asserted [S0].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default from FY2023A-FY2025A; cash balances are minimal because the group runs an overdraft-style treasury [S0].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Debt funds the capex gap while free cash flow is negative, then is repaid once capex normalises; sized to the modelled funding shortfall [S0].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests are under 1% of net profit in FY2025 and immaterial to value; held at zero [S0].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPS of Rp2.42 against EPS of Rp21.09 is an 11.5% payout; with capex still above operating cash flow we hold a token 10% payout throughout [S0].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue or buyback announced; the 2,068.5m shares have been constant since the IPO [S0].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR cash flows: below long-run nominal GDP for Indonesia (real growth plus inflation) so the terminal year does not outgrow the economy [S0].

challenges.challenge: The capex glide path, the report first value lever and the sole justification attached to the BLOCK drift flag, rests on the Ciledug hospital, which appears nowhere in the archive: not in S2, S12, S3/S6/S7 or fund record, and S12 (the cited source) is a September 2025 JawaPos piece on the Pejaten opening with no mention of Ciledug. The QC justification that capex reverts to maintenance after Ciledug is therefore unsourced.
challenges.answer: The Ciledug reference is gone: no archived source names it. The capex path and the drift.capex_pct justification now rest on the demonstrated FY2025A and 9M-2026 ratios and the balance-sheet constraint, and the report says the long-run step-down is a steady-state terminal assumption rather than a dated project [S0, S2].

challenges.challenge: Sections 1, 5 and 6 say MTMH sits on the IDX high-concentration list and was removed from the IHSG and LQ45 [S4], but S4 is a generic 383-name article whose list is published as images and whose archived text names no company, and the engine name-level registry records hsc.listed=false (source S26, asof 2026-11-11). Sections 1 and 6 also pair insider ownership of 95.0% with a free float of 11.8% (sum 106.8%), which cannot both hold and is the exact test for HSC membership.
challenges.answer: Removed the HSC/IHSG claim entirely: the name-level registry records hsc.listed=false [S26] and S4s list is an image, so the certain index risk, the HSC governance discussion and the index-eligibility signpost are deleted. Ownership now states the pack free float of 11.8%% and flags the 95.0%% insider figure as irreconcilable with it rather than pairing the two; the 30%% liquidity discount now rests on the Rp13.9m three-month ADTV [S0].

challenges.challenge: Delivered numbers are 100x wrong in key drivers: section 4 prints terminal growth as 0.0% when val.g is 4.0%; section 5 prints scenario probabilities 0.5%/0.2%/0.2% against 50/25/25; section 2 prints real GDP 529.0%, CPI 328.0% and the policy rate 575.0% against the deck 5.29/3.28/5.75. Same root cause: a pctv filter used on fractions and a pct filter used on already-percent deck values. A reader cannot reproduce the target, and the terminal-growth print makes the primary DCF look far more conservative than it is.
challenges.answer: Fixed every percent render: val.g now |pct (4.0%%), scenario probabilities |pct (50/25/25%%), deck GDP/CPI/policy rate |pctv (5.29/3.28/5.75%%), and cost-of-capital inputs kept |pctv so 10.7%% WACC prints once. All percentages now sit inside 0-100 and scenarios sum to 100%%.

challenges.challenge: Applying those weights gives Rp934 is wrong: 0.60 x 71.24 + 0.30 x 1,752.36 + 0.10 x 438.31 = Rp612.3. Rp934 is the probability-weighted scenario value (0.5 x 687.2 + 0.25 x 640.0 + 0.25 x 1,723.3). The confusion hides that the DCF contributes Rp43 of Rp612 (7%) while EV/EBITDA contributes Rp526 (86%), so the stated 60% weight to the only method that sees the capex is not what the arithmetic does. The multiple is also described as an own five-year average when own_history has n=4 (FY2022-FY2025) and its mean of 30.7x is inflated by the 47.8x of FY2023 on EBITDA of Rp69bn.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the base-case blend (weights applied to each method) and, separately, the probability-weighted figure less the liquidity discount; it says the cash flow contributes nothing after the floor and the EV/EBITDA cross-check carries the blend, and flags that the own-history mean is a four-observation average inflated by one year when EBITDA was a fraction of today's [S0].

challenges.challenge: The method card multiple-survival test and reinvestment/ROIIC discipline are absent. The DCF terminal value is Rp2,986bn, 98.0% of EV, implying an exit at 5.2x FY2035 EBITDA against 12.4x entry (EV Rp2,826bn on LTM EBITDA Rp228bn) and below every peer (lowest PRDA 5.5x). Terminal NOPAT of Rp256bn over equity plus net debt of Rp3,926bn is a 6.5% ROIC against a 10.7% WACC, so the 4% perpetual growth carrying 98% of the value is value-destructive. None of this is stated.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states that the terminal return on invested capital sits below the cost of capital, that no moat is claimed to justify terminal growth, that the terminal value is a fraction of accumulated net debt, and that the DCF equity is negative and floored at zero. The engine does not export exit-multiple or reinvestment keys, so those cannot be shown as placeholders; flagged to OPS [S0].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E is below the nine months already reported: NP Rp49.9bn against 9M actual Rp70.2bn implies a Q4 loss of Rp20.3bn, and EBITDA Rp238.2bn against 9M actual Rp215.6bn implies a Q4 margin of 5.3% against Q3 20.0%. That residual reproduces the FY2025 Q4 true-up almost exactly (gross margin 23.4%, EBIT -Rp11.2bn, NP -Rp21.1bn) because the year is anchored to FY2025A ratios, but no source says the true-up recurs. At the 9M margin on the report own FY2026 revenue of Rp1,643bn, EBITDA is Rp291bn.
challenges.answer: FY2026E is now built from the reported nine months at that period's economics: revenue, gross margin and SG&A are anchored to 9M-2026 actuals, so FY2026E net profit is above the nine-month figure and there is no implied Q4 loss and no repeat of the FY2025 true-up [S0].

challenges.challenge: The stated basis for the two margin inputs contradicts the same datapack: 9M-2026 gross margin is 31.6% (Rp384.6bn on Rp1,215.6bn) and SG&A 19.5%, not the 29.9% and 21.1% the assumption basis text claims, while FY2026E holds 29.8% and 21.3%. The combined EBIT margin is 3.7pp of revenue (about Rp60bn) below the nine months actually delivered, with no sourced step-down.
challenges.answer: The margin inputs were re-anchored: the assumption basis now states the reported 9M-2026 gross margin of 31.6% and SG&A of 19.5%, and FY2026E holds those levels rather than the FY2025A ratios the earlier text described; no sourced step-down is assumed [S0].

challenges.challenge: The report first risk is financing: cash of Rp2.7bn against debt of Rp1,022bn, interest cover about 2x, negative free cash flow through FY2030E and net debt peaking at Rp1,919.5bn. Yet no scenario contains a refinancing or covenant event and share_change is zero in every year, so the bear case (Rp640, -6.9%) excludes the risk the report itself calls impact high.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now argues the treatment explicitly: the cash-flow consequence of a tighter facility sits in the bear case as a higher cost of capital and a capex ratio that stays at the demonstrated level, while a rights issue is not modelled because no facility is disclosed as maturing, no covenant breach is disclosed and we could not date or price a raise from the material we could source. The gap is named rather than hidden [S0].

challenges.challenge: The report never recognises that the de-rating has already happened: Rp855 is 38% below the 52-week high of Rp1,390 and 12.4x LTM EV/EBITDA against the company own 16.7x at FY2025 and a 30.7x four-year mean. It builds no operating bull case from the 100-to-200-bed Pejaten expansion (F3/S12) or the cardiac and oncology mix it says supports pricing; the bull value of Rp1,723 is a scenario output with no beds, occupancy or revenue-per-bed path.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states where the shares sit in their last-year range and that the de-rating has already happened, and builds the bull case from the Pejaten beds (initial 100, expandable to 200) with the second wing equipped rather than built [S12]. We say plainly that no revenue-per-bed figure could be sourced, which is why the bull probability stays at one quarter [S0].

challenges.challenge: The scenario spread is not what the report says. EV/EBITDA and P/E are applied to LTM metrics (Rp228.0bn EBITDA, Rp49.6bn NP) that no scenario shock touches, so 40% of the target is frozen. Bear v0 (Rp569.5) is exactly base (Rp612.3) minus the DCF weighted Rp42.7, i.e. the bear case is simply the DCF worth zero; bull v0 (Rp1,533.2) requires the DCF to rise from Rp71 to Rp1,606, a 22.5x move on a -4pp capex shock. That is why mirrored inputs produce -7% and +151%, and why the probability-weighted value of Rp934 is 36% above the base case of Rp687.
challenges.answer: This is the engine's defined method, not a weighting error: m_multiple() in fund record values EV/EBITDA and P/E on the pack's LTM EBITDA and net profit, and scenario shocks apply only to model inputs and val.* overrides, so no mirrored shock can move the multiple metrics. Bear equals base once the DCF floors at zero; bull is the DCF turning positive. I removed the false claim that the asymmetry comes from the cash flow and now state the mechanic in section 5. Per-method scenario values and a multiple-metric shock require an engine change, flagged for OPS [S0].

challenges.challenge: The regulatory thesis that carries the bear narrative (omnibus law, standardised inpatient classes, KRIS) has no citation at all in section 2, whose only reference is [S0], Yahoo data; yet KRIS is the first input in the bear narrative. Separately, sections 5 and 6 say the group has acquired stakes in laboratory and pharmacy suppliers and cite [S0], whose profile text contains no acquisition disclosure.
challenges.answer: The laboratory and pharmacy acquisition claims are deleted from sections 5 and 6 because the pack does not support them. The policy discussion is confined to the numeral-free background block and section 2 now says explicitly that the implementing regulation could not be archived, so it sets no scenario weight; section 5 repeats that the regulatory risk is not one of the shocks [S0].

challenges.challenge: tax_rate of 30% is described as the three-year average, but the datapack gives FY2024 72.4% (6.96/9.62), FY2025 40.4% (29.18/72.27) and FY2023 a tax charge on a loss, for an aggregate of 55.0% (38.73/70.40). The WACC also uses a 22% marginal rate while the P&L uses 30%, so the same company is taxed two ways within one section.
challenges.answer: The 30% tax rate is gone. The P&L now uses the last actual LK effective rate of 40.4%, with the FY2024 and FY2025 derivation and the three-year aggregate stated in the assumption basis, and section 4 labels the WACC's 22% as the marginal statutory rate so the two are no longer conflated [S0].

challenges.challenge: Source hygiene is weak: S8 is titled MTMH dividends 5bn IDR but its archived text and URL are an investor.id Binance crypto-hack article; S3, S6 and S7 total 732 characters and carry no facts; fund record has six facts, none for a financial line, so every financial input rests on S0; and the accounts-filed-on-time and board/notation checks required by the earnings-quality card are asserted from S0.
challenges.answer: S8 was a mis-archive (an investor.id crypto article under a dividend title) and has been removed from the source registry, and nothing cites it now. The board, notation and filing-punctuality assertions are deleted as unsupported. A revenue fact now comes from the public-expose coverage; EBITDA, capex and net-debt facts still rest on the vendor pack because we could not retrieve the LK or annual report, which is stated in the report and flagged as thin [S2, S0].

challenges.challenge: The model accumulates cash to Rp1,119bn by FY2035 while gross debt rises to Rp2,988bn (net debt Rp1,868bn). Interest is charged at 8.9% on gross debt while cash earns 0.24%, so FY2035 net profit of Rp82.4bn is depressed by roughly Rp99bn of avoidable interest on idle cash, a capital structure no levered hospital would run.
challenges.answer: This no longer describes the model. Net borrowing turns negative in the long run, gross debt falls from its peak to a small fraction of it by FY2035 and cash is not accumulated at all; the engine charges interest on gross debt at the LK-derived rate and credits a small yield on cash, which is how the accounts behave, and the forecast shows net debt flat rather than cash piling up [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 calls the SELL 'a reduction rather than an outright short' (the rating vocabulary is REDUCE, and this name is SELL) and says 'the bear case is only mildly below the base' when the bear (Rp681) is Rp1 ABOVE the base (Rp680) - the inversion the engine WARN discloses but the text reverses.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now uses the engine's SELL vocabulary and states the inversion plainly: bear Rp681 sits a rupiah ABOVE base Rp680 because the multiple legs use LTM EBITDA and profit no shock moves and the DCF is floored, so the scenario set carries no downside expression [S0].

challenges.challenge: VAL_COMPOUNDER_QUALITY output is incomplete: section 4 gives no implied DCF exit multiple (engine terminal value implies about 1.8x FY2035E EBITDA against 12.4x entry on LTM EBITDA) and no explicit terminal reinvestment/ROIC line - the mandatory multiple-survival test (Q11).
challenges.answer: Section 4 prints the multiple-survival test: an exit near one point eight turns of FY2035E EBITDA against twelve point four times entry on LTM EBITDA, terminal reinvestment of five per cent of revenue and two-thirds of after-tax profit, ROIIC about three point seven per cent against a ten point seven per cent WACC; the summary separates the method blend from the weighted value [S0].

missing_bull_case.note: No acknowledgement that the stock is already 38% off its 52-week high (Rp1,390 to 855) and at 12.4x LTM EV/EBITDA against its own 16.7x at FY2025; no bottom-up bull path from the 100-to-200-bed Pejaten option (F3/S12) or the higher-acuity mix. The bull value is asserted, not built.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear case is base minus the DCF (Rp640, -6.9%) and contains no financing event although sections 3 and 5 rank refinancing as the top risk; no KRIS/tariff quantification and no related-party scenario, and the KRIS and supplier-acquisition arguments are uncited.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E ignores three reported quarters (NP Rp49.9bn against 9M actual Rp70.2bn) and reproduces the FY2025 Q4 true-up without a source; gross margin and SG&A are held 3.7pp of revenue below the 9M actual; the tax basis is irreproducible; the capex glide path is sourced only to an article that never mentions the project.

evidence_and_citations.note: F1-F6 all trace exactly to S2, S4 and S12, and the FY2025 arithmetic re-derives cleanly; but the Ciledug project, MTMH HSC membership and the related-party acquisitions have no valid source, S8 archives the wrong article, and no financial fact is keyed to a filing.

valuation_method_fit.note: FCFF-primary with EV/EBITDA and P/E cross-checks is the right shape for a capex-heavy hospital, but the arithmetic mislabels Rp612 as Rp934, the multiple methods supply 93% of the blend, scenarios move only the DCF, and the card exit-multiple, ROIIC and terminal-ROIC disciplines are absent (exit 5.2x against 12.4x entry; terminal ROIC 6.5% against WACC 10.7%).

bias_and_tone.note: The prose asserts more than the model does: 0.0% terminal growth printed against a 4.0% input, a fifth-per-2pp sensitivity when its own grid shows +12%/-7%, and a mirrored-scenario claim that conceals a -7%/+151% spread created by a frozen multiple weight and a zero-floored DCF.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: revenue_mode growth, IDR terminal g inside the 5.0% cap and WACC inside the 6-20% band all match the desk; but the deck is read at 100x (GDP 529.0%, CPI 328.0%, bi-rate 575.0%) and the report never states the peer set or why a 20.5x own-history/peer average is comparable to a 3.9x-levered challenger.

The 30% liquidity discount is house law from the ADTV band, and the one optimism - the unaudited 9M margin anchor - is disclosed with its Q4 arithmetic in section 3.

findings.finding: Section 4's terminal-growth paragraph says the explicit period consumes more than any terminal reading adds back. The model shows the opposite: explicit-period PV is -Rp431.5bn and discounted terminal value is +Rp451.0bn, so EV is +Rp19.5bn [S0]. The floor holds because the Rp1,057.3bn net-debt-and-minorities bridge exceeds that EV, not because the explicit period eats the terminal value; the value-driver and replacement-capex readings leave EV at about Rp1,083bn and Rp2,429bn undiscounted (about Rp529bn after discounting), both still below the bridge.

Section 4 says the value-driver terminal value is roughly a tenth below the Gordon figure. On the report's own inputs (reinvestment about two-thirds, g 2.5%, RONIC 3.7%, WACC 10.7%) the value-driver TV is Rp1,083bn against the Gordon Rp1,140bn, about 5 per cent - a twentieth, not a tenth [S0]. Direction is right; the magnitude is overstated roughly twofold in a paragraph whose purpose is to correct an earlier overstatement.

Adopted from the judge: the bull branch is valued at 9.7%, 1.3pp below the compounder card 11% IDR floor, and it is the only non-floored branch, so it lifts the probability-weighted Rp831 and the Rp582 target. Section 4 now states the direction correctly but not the size. On the engine inputs a bull branch struck at 11.0% would take roughly Rp13-25 off the target, holding the 25% bull probability [S0].
